name: Ivan Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing goes out with your name on it. I'll describe five pictures of the future and ask what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Valley Foods, the big chain supermarket in the suburbs, split between the tills and the stockroom. Three mornings a week I'm in at five taking the lorry delivery, checking pallets against the paperwork and moving them with the pallet truck. The rest of the week I'm on the tills or filling shelves. I'm still learning the stockroom system, and I've signed for the wrong pallet twice, which the manager, Derek, reminds me of.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the early deliveries, it's physical and it's done by nine. I married Lena last year, she's a receptionist at a dental practice, answering phones and booking appointments. We bought a small terrace with help from both our parents, and we've got about eight months of savings. Valley pays a bit extra for the stockroom ticket, so I'm on decent money for a junior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let people get on with their work. At work I'd joke that the AI stock system still can't stop me signing for the wrong pallet. I don't post much online, maybe something in the family group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means we carry on with the plan: work, save, start a family. Lena's job and mine both stay normal. My real goal is still to get onto the butcher's counter at Valley as an apprentice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Walter, the head butcher, if I could start the in-store butchery apprenticeship next year. I'd keep my stockroom shifts. Lena and I would keep saving and try for a baby in the next year or so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Happy, really. Things are on track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why butchery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandad was a butcher, and it's a proper skill you can be proud of. Walter's been at it thirty years and he's sharp as his knives. Butchery is the kind of job where you learn from someone, not from a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you ever use AI tools now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then, Lena showed me how to ask it to plan meals or check a recipe. It's handy. I'd use it more if I saw it actually saving me time at work.

say: I'd say good, let people get on with **their work**.
I'd joke the **stock system** still can't stop my pallet mistakes.
think: We carry on with the plan: **work, save**, start a family.
My real goal is the **butcher's counter** as an apprentice.
do: Ask Walter about the **butchery apprenticeship** next year.
Keep saving and try for a **baby** within a year.
S0.quote: Butchery is the kind of job where you learn from someone, not from a screen.
fieldNote: He values **craft skills** learned from people, like his grandad's trade.
Family plans with Lena are **on schedule** in this world.
He'd use AI more once it **proves** itself at work.

steps.text: Ask Walter about starting the butchery apprenticeship next year
Keep the early stockroom delivery shifts
Try for a first baby with Lena within a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say companies have a right to modernise, but they should train their own people. I'd say apprenticeships matter more than ever. In the family chat I'd tell everyone to learn a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My stockroom and till work change slowly, robots are slow here. The one that worries me is Lena. AI answering phones and booking appointments is exactly my wife Lena's job at the dental practice. If the dental practice cuts her hours, we lose a third of our income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard to start the butchery apprenticeship this year, not next. I'd talk to Lena about her retraining as a dental nurse, which is more hands-on. We'd hold off on a baby until we know what her job looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, more than I'd expect. Not for me, for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you and Lena talked about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Lena says the practice already tried an AI booking line and patients hated it. But they'll keep trying, because it's cheaper. I'd want her to have a plan before they get it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if her job went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. A business has to watch its costs. I'd just want the practice to offer her training first, that's the decent thing.

say: I'd say firms can modernise but should **train their own people**.
I'd tell the family that **apprenticeships** matter more than ever.
think: My work changes slowly, but **Lena's booking job** is exposed now.
If her hours go we lose **a third** of our income.
do: Start the **butchery apprenticeship** this year, not next.
**Hold off** on a baby until her job is clear.

fieldNote: The household risk sits with his **wife's desk job**, not his own.
He blames **no one**, but expects firms to offer training.
**Baby plans** are the first thing he'd delay.

steps.text: Start the in-store butchery apprenticeship this year

Put trying for a baby on hold for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for anyone to cope, and families will have to pull together. I don't think the government can fix it, but it shouldn't make it worse. I'd say young people should get into trades now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, Lena's job goes by 2028, and mine by about 2031 when robots can stack and unload. Even butchery might go by then, if robots are as good as people with their hands. I'd be scared, honestly, starting a family in that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the butchery apprenticeship anyway, because it's three years of good pay and skills. Lena would retrain as a dental nurse straight away. We'd cut back hard, no holidays, and save everything we could while we both still earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Both of us losing work in the same few years is what keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If butchery might go too, why still do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's the best thing I can do in three years, and it's a skill, not just a job. People might still want a real butcher for special cuts. And I'd rather go down learning something than just waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents, who helped with the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad we're grateful and we won't lose the house. Then I'd quietly work out how many months the savings last if we both stopped earning. About eight, which isn't a lot.

I'd say the government **shouldn't make it worse**, and youngsters need trades.
think: **Lena's job** goes by 2028, and mine by about 2031.
Starting a **family** in that world would scare me.
do: Do the **butchery apprenticeship** anyway for three good years.
Have Lena retrain as a **dental nurse** straight away.
Cut **holidays** and save everything while we both earn.
feel: **Alarmed** that we both lose work in the same few years.
S2.quote: I'd rather go down learning something than just waiting.
fieldNote: He expects **both household incomes** to fall within three years.
He still chooses a **craft skill** to use the gap before robots.
**Eight months** of savings now feels short to him.

steps.text: Begin the butchery apprenticeship within the year
Enrol Lena in dental nurse training straight away
Cancel holidays and save both wages' spare cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, but if people work hard they'll find their feet. I'd encourage apprenticeships, not handouts. At church I'd say families should look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena's job goes by about 2031, mine around 2034. That gives me time to finish butchery and have a few good years doing it. And Lena can retrain properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the apprenticeship this year and Lena would start dental nurse training next year. We'd try for a baby in two years, once she's qualified. We'd keep saving the same, not cut back hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. There's a path, it's just a narrow one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd try for a baby in two years. Isn't that right in the middle of the change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, but you can't put your life on hold for five years, and my grandparents had kids in worse times. We'd just be careful with money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI more in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, once I see Walter or Derek using it. If it helps with ordering meat or stock counts, I'd learn it. I'm not first in line, but I'm not last.

say: I'd say people who **work hard** will find their feet.
I'd back **apprenticeships**, not handouts, and families helping each other.
think: I'd have time to finish **butchery** and work a few good years.
do: Have Lena start **dental nurse** training next year.
Try for a **baby** in two years and keep saving.
S3.quote: You can't put your life on hold for five years, and my grandparents had kids in worse times.
fieldNote: Five years lets both partners **retrain in sequence**.
He refuses to **pause family life**, citing his grandparents.
He'd adopt AI after seeing **Walter or Derek** use it.

steps.text: Start the butchery apprenticeship at Valley this year

Keep the same monthly savings into the joint account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for anyone willing to work. I'd say firms should run more apprenticeships. I'd stay positive in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can be a qualified butcher for years before robots, which come around 2039, when I'm 40. Lena's job goes a bit earlier, but she'd have time to retrain. We could start a family on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the apprenticeship next year as planned. Lena would retrain within a few years, before the booking work goes. We'd try for a baby next year and keep saving steadily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. It's far enough off to plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever think of opening your own butcher's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, in five or six years. My grandad had his own shop. But I'd only do it if the town still wanted one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you, even in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena's work, still. Desk jobs go first in every one of these pictures, so I'd want my wife Lena qualified before that.

say: I'd say ten years is enough for anyone **willing to work**.
I'd push firms to run more **apprenticeships** and stay positive.
think: I can be a **qualified butcher** for years before 2039.
Lena has time to **retrain** before booking work goes.
do: Start the **apprenticeship** next year as planned.
S4.quote: Desk jobs go first in every one of these pictures, so I'd want my wife Lena qualified before that.
fieldNote: Ten years lets his **family plans** stay on time.
He dreams of a **shop of his own**, like his grandad's.
His lasting worry is always **Lena's desk job**.

steps.text: Start the butchery apprenticeship next year
Try for a first baby with Lena next year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Lena and I could both lose our jobs within three years of each other. What would help is apprenticeships for adults that pay a real wage, and companies being made to train their own staff first. That, and family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my wife's job much. People think shop workers are the ones at risk, but the phones and the booking desks go first. Lena's more exposed than me.

headlineQuote: People think shop workers are the ones at risk, but the phones and the booking desks go first.
portrait: Ivan is a **27-year-old** till and stockroom worker at a suburban chain supermarket.
He and his wife Lena, a **dental receptionist**, own a small terrace and have eight months saved.
He wants a **butchery apprenticeship**, a craft his grandad practised.
He's calm in AI Plateau but **alarmed** by AGI by 2028, because both incomes fall.
He backs **apprenticeships** over handouts and adopts new tools once proven.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with both his and Lena's jobs gone within three years.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid adult apprenticeships** at a real wage.
Firms required to **train their own staff** first.
